the G-rich repetitive DNA sequences, such as minisatellites and telomeres, are maintained by the formation of G4 structures, and that the G-rich triplet repeats, such as d(CGG), are also maintained by the formation and resolution of higher order structures.

G-rich repetitive sequences form secondary structures and that hnRNPs, which are tightly and specifically bound, may contribute to the formation of the G4' structures and the maintenance of the repetitive sequences.

In summary, our research is concerned with
the molecular mechanisms underlying maintenance of G-rich repeats that can adopt a G4 structure.
the molecular mechanisms underlying the maintenance of G4 DNA structure-forming repeats.
the elucidation of molecular mechanisms for maintenance of the G-rich repeat sequences, which may be important for the prevention of human diseases.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
hnRNP A family proteins are the key players in maintaining G-rich repetitive sequences and in regulating gene transcription.

G-rich repetitive sequences form various secondary DNA structures that can be recognized and resolved by specific proteins, including hnRNP A/B, and that this may play important roles in the maintenance of the genome in normal cells and the pathophysiology of several human disorders.

the hnRNP A family of proteins, especially hnRNP A2, A1 and A0, may be involved in the regulation and maintenance of G4' structures formed in the repetitive sequences, including minisatellites and telomeres, in mammalian cells.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
hnRNPs may play a key role in the maintenance of G4 DNA structures and the stability of the human genome.
the G4 structures of the repetitive sequences in the genome are maintained by hnRNPs and the G4 structure is a key to the preferential mutagenesis of these repeats.
hnRNP proteins may play important roles in the regulation of the genome by maintaining the G-rich short tandem repetitive sequences.
The main takeaway from our work is that
G4 DNA structures are formed by G-rich repetitive sequences in the genome and the formation of these structures is tightly regulated in vivo.
G-rich repeats can adopt G4 DNA structures in the genome, and these G4 DNA structures can be recognized by hnRNP A proteins.

the G4 DNA structures formed by the repetitive sequences may be involved in the mutational hotspots of these repetitive sequences, and that hnRNP A family proteins play an important role in the maintenance of the repetitive sequences.
